page_hint: §4 'Boundary rule' paragraph; §6 'Inference scaling' paragraph; §8 fallback-ledger paragraph
quoted_clause: **Boundary rule.** A call's *input* never contains *its own* output tokens (a later call's input does carry earlier calls' outputs and tool results — which is exactly why Σ per-call inputs double-counts carried context and exceeds the retained 12,095), so `task_input` must sum per-call inputs only — never the “Total tokens (incl. 300 output)” column (10,365 / 11,230 / 12,095 / 12,960 are *retained context + final output*, i.e. the α and Ch 17 KV quantities).

Apply the same treatment to the §4 Boundary rule and the §6 Inference scaling paragraph.

page_hint: §4 'Scope note' paragraph; §8 'Architectural actions' paragraph

correction: Add to §8's 'Architectural actions': 'With prefix caching enabled, the fleet-sizing basis becomes W(3) ≈ 14.14 s rather than 17.70 s; Ch 17 §8 carries both columns — the architect must state which one the host count assumes, because the two differ by the concurrency effect described in §6.'
acceptance_test: Ch 19 states which W value its own recommended configuration implies, and cross-references the matching Ch 17 column.

page_hint: §8 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger' table, fallback row and lead-in
quoted_clause: guardrail evaluation + re-dispatch adds ~200 ms
observed: The fallback row's added orchestration (860 ms) charges the three attempted turns (660 ms) plus 200 ms for guardrail evaluation and re-dispatch, but the re-dispatch itself is a fresh model invocation that would incur its own orchestration step (λ_step ≈ 120 ms per §4). The 200 ms term is therefore either understated or is meant to include the re-dispatch's orchestration — the text does not say which.
evidence: §4: λ_step ≈ 120 ms is 'per-invocation system overhead — scheduling, KV-cache slot allocation, kernel launch'. The fallback path contains four model invocations (three attempts + one single-shot), so four orchestration steps are incurred, not three.
root_cause: The fallback's invocation count was not reconciled with the per-invocation overhead definition.
correction: State the composition explicitly: 'the fallback incurs four model invocations and therefore four orchestration steps (4 × 120 ms = 480 ms) plus three tool legs (3 × 100 ms = 300 ms) plus ~200 ms of guardrail evaluation — i.e. ≈980 ms — or, if the 200 ms term is intended to include the re-dispatch's step overhead, say so and adjust the row.'
acceptance_test: The fallback row's added-orchestration figure equals the number of model invocations in that class times λ_step, plus the number of tool legs times λ_tool, plus any stated extra term.

page_hint: §8 'Scenario' paragraph; §6 'Inference scaling' paragraph
quoted_clause: An enterprise RQA system serves 2,000 knowledge workers.

page_hint: §6 'Task economics' paragraph, following the equation

page_hint: §3 'Scope note on the turn cap'; §4 turn-distribution paragraph; §8 'Measurement results'
quoted_clause: The *recommended operational* policy — deployed in the §8 mini-case and used for fleet sizing in Chapter 17 — caps turns at 3, per the §4 guidance and the 95th-percentile sizing rule (size for the 95th-percentile turn count — §4's illustrative distribution gives p95 T = 3)
observed: The cap is derived from the p95 of a turn distribution that is itself defined under the cap. §8's telemetry is 'the scenario's 30-day telemetry' from a system whose 'maximum of 3 turns' is already in force, so the observed distribution is censored at T = 3 and the '2% exceed the turn limit' class is by construction, not an observation. Using a censored distribution's p95 to set the cap is circular: the rule can only be applied to an uncensored distribution.
evidence: §8: 'The team introduces an agentic layer with a maximum of 3 turns' and 'The scenario's 30-day telemetry shows ... 2% exceed the turn limit and fall back to single-shot'. §4: 'the illustrative turn distribution here has ... 95th percentile T = 3 ... derived from the §8 distribution'. The §8 distribution is therefore the output of the policy that the distribution is used to set.
root_cause: The sizing rule was stated without its measurement precondition; the illustrative distribution was allowed to stand in for the uncensored one.
correction: State the precondition explicitly: 'The 95th-percentile sizing rule requires an *uncensored* turn distribution — measured with the cap disabled, or from a shadow run — because a distribution observed under a cap of 3 is truncated at 3 and its p95 cannot be used to choose the cap. The distribution used here is illustrative and should be read as an uncensored one.'
acceptance_test: Ch 19 states how the turn distribution used for cap selection is obtained, and flags that §8's telemetry is censored by the policy it supports.

page_hint: Ch 20 §3, subsection 'KV-residency / latency bound (Little's Law)' (the paragraph beginning 'The binding per-host rate is the *minimum* of the two')
quoted_clause: The binding per-host rate is the *minimum* of the two — here the KV/latency bound.
observed: The chapter states that the KV/latency bound is the binding per-host rate, but its own subsequent analysis shows a third bound (the prefill-compute screen) that binds above the KV bound under case (ii) and ties it under case (iii). The 'minimum of the two' framing also omits the prefill-only token-throughput bound (19,780/9,200 = 2.15 req/s under case (i); 16,870/9,200 = 1.83 req/s under case (ii)), which is the bound that actually governs fleet size.
evidence: Re-derived from the chapter's own numbers: KV bound = 17/8.6 = 1.977 req/s/host. Prefill-only ceiling case (i) = 19,780 tokens/s ÷ 9,200 = 2.150 req/s/host; case (iii) = 18,210/9,200 = 1.979 req/s/host; case (ii) = 16,870/9,200 = 1.834 req/s/host. Under case (ii) the prefill bound (1.834) is strictly below the KV bound (1.977), and the chapter's own fleet screen gives 22 hosts (prefill) > 21 hosts (KV). The 'Simultaneous feasibility check' subsection also reports 18,400/16,870 ≈ 109% (case ii) and ≈101% (case iii), i.e. prefill alone does not fit at 2 req/s under those conventions.
root_cause: The 'minimum of two bounds' template was written before the prefill-compute screen (cases i/ii/iii) was added to the chapter; the later material was appended rather than integrated into the bound-selection logic.
correction: Restate the bound selection as a minimum over three named bounds — KV-slot (1.977 req/s/host), prefill-compute (case-dependent: 2.150 / 1.979 / 1.834 req/s/host), and phase-mixed token throughput (3.684 req/s/host, non-comparable) — and state explicitly that the KV bound binds under cases (i) and (iii) while the case-(ii) prefill bound binds (hence 22 hosts, and 23 with the ρ derate). Move the 'Simultaneous feasibility check' immediately before the bound-selection sentence so the reader sees the third bound before the conclusion that names the binding one.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, for each of cases (i)/(ii)/(iii), which bound binds and why; no sentence in §3 asserts the KV bound binds while the chapter's own tables show a larger requirement under case (ii).

page_hint: Ch 20 §3, 'Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form)' (paragraphs 'Separately, the independent prefill compute screen…' and 'The correct statement is: the fleet must satisfy every named screen…'); also Ch 20 §8 mini-case, 'Planning-bound caveat (sizing tail)'
quoted_clause: the independent prefill compute screen (Ch. 8, 35% MFU) gives **19 hosts under case (i)** (⌈18.60⌉, linear-only), **21 under case (iii)** (⌈20.21⌉, causal-triangle) and **22 under case (ii)** (⌈21.81⌉, full-square conservative) … The correct statement is: the fleet must satisfy every named screen, and the *larger* requirement wins — **21 hosts under case (i), 22 under case (ii)**

The result is a direct numeric collision inside one paragraph: '19 hosts under case (i)' (prefill screen) and '21 hosts under case (i)' (KV screen) both appear, and the mini-case writes '21 = KV screen under case (i)'.
evidence: Both quoted sentences are in the same subsection. The KV screen is ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 regardless of FLOP convention; the prefill screen is 19/21/22 under cases (i)/(iii)/(ii). The mini-case's parenthetical '21 = KV screen under case (i); 22 = the ρ ≈ 0.95 derate of that screen; 23 = the ρ-derated full-square case (ii) prefill compute screen' attaches a FLOP-convention label to a screen that has no FLOP content.
root_cause: Case labels were introduced for the Ch 8 prefill FLOP conventions and then reused as a global 'scenario' label for the whole screen set, without renaming the prefill-only cases.
correction: Rename the FLOP conventions explicitly as 'prefill FLOP convention (i) linear-only / (ii) full-square / (iii) causal-triangle' and never attach them to the KV screen. Rewrite the summary as: 'KV screen: 21 hosts (case-independent); prefill screen: 19 (i) / 21 (iii) / 22 (ii); max over screens: 21 (i), 21 (iii), 22 (ii).' Update the mini-case caveat and the Fig 20.1 caption/note accordingly.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 20 pairs 'case (i)/(ii)/(iii)' with the KV screen; a reader can map every host-count number in the chapter to exactly one screen and one convention.

page_hint: Ch 20 §1 'Concept' (key-concept bullet 'Autoscaling break-even'); Ch 20 §3 'Autoscaling economics'; Ch 20 §7 'Economic auto-scaling'
quoted_clause: **Autoscaling break-even**: The point at which growth in SLO-good requests covers the next host's fixed cost — *average* cost per query falls as fixed costs amortize, while marginal cost per query stays roughly constant.
observed: One of the three named key concepts of the chapter is never operationalized. No fixed-overhead term is ever quantified, no average-cost-per-request curve is computed, and no break-even point is derived. §3 gives only the marginal cost ($20 ÷ 1.977 ≈ $10.12 per req/s per hour) and explicitly declines the average-cost computation; §7 then lists 'Economic auto-scaling' as an open question. The reader leaves the chapter with a named concept and no instance of it.
evidence: Search of the chunk: the only cost quantities are $20/hr cloud, $8/hr owned, $10.12 per req/s per hour, $0.08 (hypothetical), $0.012 (Ch 4 per-request API price). No value is assigned to 'model loading, infrastructure, staff' (the fixed overhead named in §1), so average cost per request and its break-even cannot be computed from anything the chapter states.
root_cause: The Concept section promised an economic concept that the Worked Example section narrowed to a marginal-cost calculation; the two were never reconciled.
correction: Either (a) operationalize: add a short average-cost worked line, e.g. with an explicit [ASSUMPTION] fixed overhead F per hour, average cost per request = (F + 20N)/(1.977·N·3600) and the utilization at which the owned fleet ($8/hr) beats on-demand ($20/hr) — which the chapter's own numbers already fix at 40% — and state the break-even explicitly; or (b) demote 'Autoscaling break-even' from a key concept to a §7 open question and keep §1's marginal/average distinction only.
acceptance_test: Either the chapter contains a computed break-even with stated inputs, or 'autoscaling break-even' no longer appears as a key concept in §1.

page_hint: Ch 20 §1 (unit convention sentence); §2 ('the fleet must sustain **~40 requests/s at peak**'); §3 ('Keeping the illustrative per-host rps = Q'; 'Evaluated at the displayed ~2.0 rps'); §4 Table 20-1 row 'Aggregate rps'; §8 ('≥ 2× peak = 80 rps')
quoted_clause: Unit convention for this chapter: *rps* denotes an arrival rate and *req/s* a capacity rate; both are requests per second.
observed: The chapter's own stated unit convention is violated in at least five places: an arrival rate is written as 'requests/s' (§2), a capacity rate is written as 'rps' (§3 'per-host rps = Q', §3 'the displayed ~2.0 rps', §4 'Aggregate rps', §8 '80 rps').
evidence: §2: 'the fleet must sustain **~40 requests/s at peak**' — 40 rps is the arrival rate (Ch 4 Table 4-2), so per the stated convention it should read '~40 rps'. §3: 'Keeping the illustrative per-host rps = Q' — Q is a capacity rate (17/8.6), so it should be 'req/s'. §3: 'Evaluated at the displayed ~2.0 rps' — 2.0 req/s is a capacity rate. §4 Table 20-1: 'Aggregate rps | Total queries processed per second across all hosts' — a capacity rate. §8: '≥ 2× peak = 80 rps is a stress/soak target' — a capacity rate.
root_cause: The convention was introduced in §1 and then not enforced; the two symbols were treated as interchangeable in drafting.
correction: Enforce the convention everywhere: arrival rates (10 rps average, 40 rps peak, 80 rps soak target as an offered load) use 'rps'; capacity rates (2.0 req/s per host, 41.5 rps fleet capacity, 15.8 req/s for 8 hosts) use 'req/s'. Where a figure axis or table column mixes them, label the column 'req/s (capacity)' or 'rps (arrival)'.
acceptance_test: A grep of Ch 20 shows every occurrence of 'rps' attached to an arrival/offered rate and every occurrence of 'req/s' attached to a capacity rate, with no exceptions in §2, §3, §4, or §8.

page_hint: Ch 20 §8 mini-case, 'Solution' opening parenthetical vs the first bullet
quoted_clause: **Solution** (illustrative algebra — the per-host figure is an [ILLUSTRATIVE] estimate for showing the fleet math; …) … So C/W = 17 / 8.6 = 1.977 ≈ **2.0 requests/s** [ANALYTICAL] at steady state
observed: The same quantity (the per-host 1.977 req/s) carries two different evidence labels within the same solution block: [ILLUSTRATIVE] in the framing sentence and [ANALYTICAL] in the bullet. The house taxonomy treats [ILLUSTRATIVE] and [ANALYTICAL] as distinct provenance/status values; one distribution must carry one label.
evidence: §3 labels the identical expression 'C/W = 17 / 8.6 = 1.977 ≈ **2.0 requests/s** [ANALYTICAL]'. The mini-case's framing sentence downgrades it to [ILLUSTRATIVE] while the bullet restores [ANALYTICAL].
root_cause: The framing sentence was written to hedge the whole solution (the fleet algebra is illustrative) and accidentally relabeled the per-host figure, which is in fact an analytical derivation from Ch 17's KV ceiling.
correction: Label the per-host rate [ANALYTICAL] everywhere (it is derived from Ch 17's KV ceiling and an assumed residency), and label the *fleet sizing conclusions* [ILLUSTRATIVE] (they depend on the assumed arrival profile and the ρ derate). If the intent was to mark the whole mini-case illustrative, use a single scope label on the 'Solution' heading rather than relabeling the inner quantity.
acceptance_test: The string '17 / 8.6 = 1.977' carries exactly one label in every place it appears in Ch 20.

page_hint: Ch 20 §4 Table 20-1 (rows 'Scheduler-added p99 latency', 'Scheduling overhead'); §3 'Scheduling overhead'; §8 mini-case bullet on the 100-ms p99
quoted_clause: **Scheduler-added p99 latency** | 99th-percentile time a request waits in the fleet dispatcher (NOT end-to-end — model execution is multi-second here) | < 100 ms … the dispatcher's added p99 overhead is specified as `≤ 5% of the request time on the same request population`
observed: Two different dispatch-overhead specifications coexist: Table 20-1 sets a p99 dispatch latency target of < 100 ms, while §3 and the mini-case specify '≤ 5% of the request time'. For the canonical 8.6 s service time, 5% is 430 ms — four times looser than the table's 100 ms. A reader cannot tell which is the governing target.
evidence: 5% × 8,580 ms = 429 ms. Table 20-1 target = 100 ms. §3: 'it must stay under ~5% of the *measured* per-request time'. §8: 'the dispatcher's added p99 overhead is specified as `≤ 5% of the request time on the same request population`'.
root_cause: The table was written as an absolute-latency SLO; the worked example expressed the same idea as a fraction of service time, and the two were never reconciled.
correction: Make one primary and one derived: state the primary target as an absolute p99 dispatch latency (< 100 ms, Table 20-1) and note that for the canonical 8.6 s service time this corresponds to ≈ 1.2% of request time, i.e. comfortably inside the ≤ 5% rule of thumb. Or, if the fraction is the intended primary, restate the table target as '< 100 ms (≈ 1.2% of the canonical 8.6 s request time)'. Apply the same statement in §3 and §8.
acceptance_test: A reader can state the dispatch-overhead target in one sentence and can tell whether the 100 ms and 5% figures are the same constraint or two.

page_hint: Ch 20 §5 'Common Mistakes', first bullet
quoted_clause: **Treating hosts as independent**: Optimizing each host in isolation (e.g., tuning batch size per host) ignores the scheduling overhead that becomes dominant when the fleet is viewed as a unit.
observed: The mistake's justification contradicts the chapter's own numbers: §3 states dispatch overhead is 'negligible next to a real 7.5 s decode' (~0.5 ms vs 8,580 ms ≈ 0.006%), and Table 20-1 targets < 5%. The chapter never shows scheduling overhead becoming dominant. The second sentence's causal chain is also a non sequitur: a suboptimal batch size on one host does not cause the scheduler to re-balance 'more often … for the entire fleet'.
evidence: §3: 'A lightweight round-robin scheduler adds ~0.5 ms of dispatch latency per request [ILLUSTRATIVE] — negligible next to a real 7.5 s decode'. Table 20-1: 'Scheduling overhead | Fraction of per-query time spent in dispatcher, not compute | < 5%'. 0.5 ms / 8,580 ms = 0.006%.
root_cause: The Common Mistakes bullet was written from a general 'fleet effects matter' intuition rather than from the chapter's measured magnitudes; the specific mechanism asserted (dispatch-decision rate rising fleet-wide) was never derived.
correction: Rewrite the mistake around the effect the chapter actually supports: per-host misconfiguration creates *variance* in per-host service time and completion rate, which inflates fleet-level tail latency and utilization variance (Table 20-1's 'Utilization variance < 0.2') even when aggregate capacity is ample — the §2 'Poor placement can cause some hosts to saturate while others remain underutilized, inflating the 99th-percentile latency' mechanism. Remove the claim that dispatch overhead 'becomes dominant' and the unsupported re-balancing-frequency claim, or replace it with the measured-dispatch-rate argument (dispatch decisions per second scale with arrival rate, not with per-host batch tuning).
acceptance_test: No sentence in §5 asserts a magnitude that contradicts §3 or Table 20-1; the stated mechanism is one the chapter has actually established.

page_hint: Ch 20 §3, 'Throughput bound (tokens/s)' vs 'Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form)' (bullet 'Token-throughput screen → 11 hosts (non-binding)')
quoted_clause: **These two are not directly comparable as single numbers** … what makes the division wrong here is what its numerator mixes and its answer assumes, not its units. … **Token-throughput screen → 11 hosts (non-binding).** The token-throughput ceiling gives ⌈40 / 3.684⌉ = 11 hosts
observed: The chapter first argues at length that dividing the phase-mixed 35,000 tokens/s by tokens-per-request is invalid (no cost/phase-equivalence model), then performs exactly that division and reports a host count (11) as one of the fleet screens. The screen is presented with the same visual weight as the valid screens.
evidence: §3 'Throughput bound': 'Dividing the total by the ~9,500 tokens/request gives ~3.7 requests/s — **but this is not achievable here**'. §3 'Fleet aggregate throughput': '**Token-throughput screen → 11 hosts (non-binding).** The token-throughput ceiling gives ⌈40 / 3.684⌉ = 11 hosts'. 40/3.684 = 10.86 → 11.
root_cause: The invalid-division argument was added after the host-count screen had already been written, and the screen was not downgraded when the argument landed.
correction: Either remove the 11-host screen (it adds no information: it is non-binding by a factor of ~2 and rests on a numerator the chapter rejects), or keep it but label it explicitly as a non-comparable upper edge, e.g. 'phase-mixed token-throughput edge (not a screen; the numerator mixes phases — see above)'. Do not present it in the same screen list as the KV and prefill screens.
acceptance_test: No host count in Ch 20 is derived from a numerator the chapter has declared invalid without an explicit non-comparability label.

page_hint: Ch 20 §7 'What We Still Don't Know', bullet 'Cross-query caching effects'
quoted_clause: In RAG workloads, the ~9,200 in-tokens and ~300 out-tokens per query overlap significantly across users asking related questions. The potential for caching intermediate embeddings or partial KV caches is substantial, but the cost of cache management (invalidation, coherence, metadata overhead) must be quantified against the compute savings.
observed: The open question conflates three different things and proposes one that is not a meaningful compute saving. (a) Output-token overlap is not a caching opportunity in the sense described: outputs are model-generated, and 'overlap' between two users' answers is a quality/answer-reuse question, not a KV-reuse question. (b) 'Caching intermediate embeddings' saves essentially nothing: embeddings are a deterministic, cheap function of the token IDs (a lookup plus one GEMM), so caching them removes a negligible fraction of prefill compute — the savings live in the transformer blocks, not the embedding table. (c) 'Partial KV caches' is a real mechanism (prefix caching) already covered elsewhere in the book, so as an open question it is misplaced.
evidence: The chapter's own prefill arithmetic (Ch 8, 35% MFU) attributes prefill cost to 2 × 70e9 FLOP/token in the transformer blocks; the embedding lookup is not in that term. The chapter's §5 'Overlooking data movement cost' already treats the retrieved context as the shared artifact.
root_cause: The bullet was drafted as a generic 'caching is under-explored' gesture rather than from the chapter's own resource model.
correction: Rewrite the bullet to name the actual open quantity: the *prefix-overlap distribution* of RAG prompts (how many leading tokens are shared across concurrent queries, and therefore what fraction of prefill FLOPs prefix caching can remove), and the cache-management cost (eviction, coherence, metadata) that must be charged against it. Drop the output-token overlap framing or restate it as answer-level reuse (a product/semantics question, not a serving-system one), and drop 'caching intermediate embeddings' or explain why it is not a compute saving.
acceptance_test: Each caching mechanism named in §7 maps to a resource in the chapter's own model (bytes, FLOPs, or memory) and to a measurable quantity.
